newsitem.title: USA: Democratic senator charges cave-in on gun control.
newsitem.headline: Democratic senator charges cave-in on gun control.

text.p: A key Democratic senator charged Wednesday that Republicans were poised to give in to the National Rifle Association and let child-abusers keep their guns, reversing a one-sided Senate vote on gun control.

Gun control is one of several issues being negotiated between Republicans and Democrats as part of an omnibus spending bill they intend to pass to keep the government funded after the Oct. 1 start of the new fiscal year.

Sen. Frank Lautenberg, a New Jersey Democrat, said the Senate-passed bill to ban gun ownership by child- and spouse-abusers was being substantially weakened in negotiations with the House at the urging of Republicans opposed to gun control.

"It will jeopardise the lives of thousands of battered women and children around the nation," he said on the Senate floor. "I know the NRA has a lot of power around here. But isn't there some point at which we draw the line?"

The House has not approved the gun control bill that cleared the Senate by 97-2 on Sept. 12 as an amendment to the Treasury Department's 1997 funding. The entire bill was pulled before a final vote because of disagreements over other issues.

Lawmakers reported they were near agreement on all spending issues, including the approximately $6.5 billion President Clinton wanted for schools, illegal drug control and anti-terrorist measures. But policy issues still divide them.
"Money is not an issue," Senate Appropriations Committee chairman Mark Hatfield, R-Oregon, told reporters after a meeting with House Speaker Newt Gingrich, R-Georgia.

Lautenberg said he would use "all the tools at my disposal" to fight changes in the gun ban. These tools could include the threat to hold up passage of the spending bill. Congress must vote by Oct. 1 to fund government agencies for 1997 or risk another unpopular government closure.
The proposed new gun control language would also allow spousal abusers to keep their guns if they were convicted by a judge in what is known as a bench trial rather than in a trial by jury.

And spousal abusers would be given an added civil right. At the time they were charged with abuse, they would have to be warned of the possible loss of a right to own guns. If the warning were not delivered, they could keep their guns even if convicted.
Accused criminals must be warned of their rights to keep silent and to have an attorney.

In more than 30 states, battering a spouse or child is considered a misdemeanor, a crime punishable by no more than a year in jail. In those same states, phyiscal attack on a neighbour or a neighbour's child is a felony, a crime punishable by more than a year in jail.

Sen. Paul Wellstone, D-Minnesota, noted recently that the vast majority of the 2 million cases of spousal abuse each year involve the battering of wives or former wives and in 150,000 cases a gun was present.
The House earlier this year killed the gun-control measure when passed by the Senate as part of an anti-stalking bill.
